NVIDIA to Unveil "Pascal" at the 2016 Computex

I use mostly NVIDIA products at work and home, but I don't choose them because of their hardware. They are primarily a software company that focuses on clients and developers. Their software, drivers and debugging tools, generally works fantastic. Their hardware is actually mostly meh for a high cost.

AMD it's pretty much the opposite on the GPU spectrum. Good hardware, shit for drivers and debugging tools. This is pretty much why NVIDIA makes a better choice for a PC GPU and AMD makes perfect sense for console manufactures to use them for their GPUs.

Then you have mobile GPUs. Imagination has far and away the best battery life to GPU throughput ratio, but it comes with some strict limitations and an extra frame of delay from draw call submission to seeing something on screen. Qualcomm bought ATI's retired GPU that was based on the X360 GPU. Fairly versatile hardware, a decade ago, but improved a little bit. Absolutely abysmal driver support though. The Mali GPU is a dinosaur in architecture last time I talked to vendors around 18 months ago. It was still vector-based and not scalar. Unfortunately, it's cheap/popular and it's a crapshoot in many devices if you'll get a Qualcomm Adreno GPU or a Mali GPU, even if it is labeled as the same device (ex- Galaxy Note 5) and even if it has the same fucking part numbers.

Well, up for some console responses? I'll start at the Wii and move forward. Stop me if you're not interested.

Wii: Basically 2 gamecubes strapped together with some extra memory. PowerPC, so the endian-ness is swapped from your actual PC (0xff000000 is now 0x000000ff). Annoying, but you deal with it. (this concept is dead as of current hardware AFAIK. I have not done a WiiU game to verify this.)

Anyways, more Wii stuff. The OS library for system actions (file IO, threading, etc) was pretty much identical to what was on the GameCube and still identical to what was on the N64. Nintendo is really bad about updating this shit. Literally the N64 docs were more helpful than the Wii docs in some areas. The Wii you did not really have shaders, you had 'tev' stages. You had up to 8 stages where you could blend texture information or vertex information to create the output result. The Wii also had the indirect Tev, where you could modify the UVs (the texel of a texture you want to read) to create unique effects. That was useful for things like water or heat, where you could fake reflection/refration/etc.

PSP - Worst console in history to work on. Hardware had an 8kb texture cache, so all textures literally had to fit into that, or smaller. Had no polygon clipping, so say you had a triangle that was large and went off screen - you had to literally clip it and create new triangles yourself on the separate FPU (floating point unit - a co-processor), or overly tessellate your geometry. We did the latter and shipped the game at 15fps due to that. Manually clipping was far more expensive for a 3d game than tessellating our geo.

PS3 - My bread and butter. I literally spent years of my life optimizing for this console. I moved the obvious final post processing phase to the SPUs - bloom, tone mapping, color correction (LUTs), MLAA, etc. - but also moved mid frame effects like SSAO to the SPUs. It was basically writing vectorized assembly to go graphics shit. Naughty Dog took it far further to do triangle culling and submission from the SPUs, but I spend a good 2 years of my life just doing the former....mostly due to API bugs and having to rewrite the system several times to accomodate for those bugs.

Now the PS3 GPU - The RSX - an NVIDIA GPU. This was an awful GPU, just as the PPU was an awful CPU. You had to literally manually patch shader programs with their shader constants before uploading them to the GPU. Basically, if the sun moved slightly, you might have to upload a new 10kb patch to the GPU to render an object. New, and even old, hardware just puts that information in dedicated registers. The PS3 was literally a frankenstein. Also...GPAD - the debugging tool. You get great analytic information with literally hundreds of tokens of what is stressing the GPU here and there....but none of them have any documentation telling you what they actually mean. Any PS3 developer can verify this.

Skipping some stuff, now the X360. Literally, this console was god's gift to man. You compile your code, you give it a directory on your PC, and you can run the game. Unfathomably, it worked perfectly. No game console ever did this before. Seriously. [Meta - It's far better than the XBone or PS4 dev tools today]. XBox PIX is amazing for graphics debugging, easy enough for artists to use.

OK fast forward 8 years. The XBone and PS4. The XBone has literally worse developer tools than the PS2 had. Microsoft took a C# team and put them on the XBone while putting the Xbox 360 team on something else. Many walls were destroyed from heads banging on them due to awful decisions being made by a literally bad team. XBone PIX is ok, but it's a 13k line text dump where it does not explain what shit like "bus transactions" mean, or how to prevent them.

PS4 comes about. We literally have the driver implemtation of DX12. Shit starts making sense why DX11 was literally an awfully designed API (seriously....if you get anything out of this article, DX11 was a horribly designed API - they kicked out the advisory council during DX11 and just did what the heck ever. Metal/Mantle/Vulcan/DX12 start making sense. 99% of your cost is building these massive tables that say "this draw call wants to read info from these pointers". Literally, that's it. That's what new APIs give you control of. Caching that info is basically god.

Anyways, I need to sleep, so I'll probably be up another 3 hours.
